How can I revise?

Create mind maps for key characters (Mickey, Eddie, Mrs Johnstone, Linda)
Revise the key themes: Class, hope, gender, nature vs nurture

flashcards.back: Willy Russell. It is a musical play set in Liverpool.
A poor, working-class single mother of many children. She works as a cleaner for Mrs Lyons. She gives away one of her twins.
The twin who stays with Mrs Johnstone. He grows up working class. Later he loses his job, goes to prison and becomes depressed.
The twin given to Mrs Lyons. He grows up middle class, goes to university and becomes a councillor.
A wealthy woman who cannot have children. She persuades Mrs Johnstone to give her one twin. She becomes anxious and paranoid.
A friend of both twins since childhood. She marries Mickey.
A character who comments on the action and reminds the audience about fate and the ending.
Mickey's older brother. He gets into trouble and leads Mickey into crime.
Mickey and Eddie become 'blood brothers' as children. They do not know they are really twins.
The twins have very different lives because of the class they grow up in. Money gives Eddie chances that Mickey never gets.
Characters dream of a better life, but their hopes are often crushed by money worries and class.
Women in the play, like Mrs Johnstone and Linda, have few choices and depend on men and money.
The twins are born the same (nature) but grow up in different homes (nurture). The play suggests upbringing shapes their lives.
Mrs Lyons invents a superstition that twins separated at birth will die if they learn the truth. The Narrator keeps hinting at this fate.
Using the same word or phrase more than once to make an idea stand out.
Words chosen to make the reader or audience feel strong emotions, such as sadness or anger.
Saying something IS something else, to compare them. For example: 'Time is a thief.'
Speaking straight to someone, often using 'you'.
Three dots (…) that show words are left out or a thought trails off. It can create tension or sadness.
Comparing two things using 'like' or 'as'. For example: 'as cold as ice'.
A hint early in a story about something that will happen later.
When the audience knows something that a character does not know.
Feeling sorry for a character and understanding how they feel.
Working out something the writer suggests but does not say directly.

quiz.q: "The classroom was a zoo." Which technique is this?
quiz.explain: It says the classroom IS a zoo, without 'like' or 'as'.

quiz.q: "Her voice was as soft as a feather." Which technique is this?
quiz.explain: It compares using 'as … as'.

quiz.q: "Never, never, never give up." Which technique is this?
quiz.explain: The word 'never' is used three times for emphasis.

quiz.q: "You know how it feels to wait." Which technique is this?
quiz.explain: The speaker talks straight to 'you'.

quiz.q: "I thought he would come back…" What does the ellipsis (…) suggest?
options: A thought trailing off, perhaps sadly
quiz.explain: Ellipsis shows words left unsaid, often sadness or doubt.

quiz.q: "The heartbroken child sobbed alone in the freezing dark." Which technique is used most?
quiz.explain: Words like 'heartbroken', 'sobbed' and 'alone' are chosen to make us feel sad.

quiz.q: Early in a story, a character says: "Nothing bad will ever happen here." Later something terrible happens. What was the early line?
quiz.explain: It hints at what will happen later.

quiz.q: The audience knows a letter is fake, but the character believes it. What is this called?
quiz.explain: The audience knows something the character does not.

quiz.q: "Hope is a candle in a storm." Which technique is this?
quiz.explain: It says hope IS a candle.

quiz.q: "Run like the wind!" Which technique is this?
quiz.explain: It compares using 'like'.

quiz.q: "Listen to me, please. Just listen." Which TWO techniques are used here?
quiz.explain: The speaker talks to someone directly and repeats 'listen'.

quiz.q: "The bills piled up, cruel and endless, crushing the family." Which technique is this?
quiz.explain: Words like 'cruel' and 'crushing' make us feel the family's pain.

quiz.q: Where is Blood Brothers set?
quiz.explain: The play is set in Liverpool.

quiz.q: Why does Mrs Johnstone agree to give away a twin?
options: She is poor and cannot afford another child
quiz.explain: She is already struggling for money with many children.

quiz.q: Which twin is brought up by Mrs Lyons?
quiz.explain: Eddie (Edward) grows up in the wealthy Lyons family.

quiz.q: Which theme is about upbringing shaping who you become?
quiz.explain: The twins share nature but have different nurture.

quiz.q: In the page 5 extract, how does Mrs Johnstone enter?
quiz.explain: The stage direction at the top of the extract tells you. Check it in your booklet.

quiz.q: In the page 5 extract, what is Mrs Johnstone mostly worried about?
options: Losing her baby and money troubles
quiz.explain: She worries about debts and about not being allowed to keep the baby.

quiz.q: What does Linda do later in the play?
quiz.explain: Linda marries Mickey.

quiz.q: Which theme is shown by Eddie going to university while Mickey loses his job?
quiz.explain: Money and class give Eddie chances that Mickey does not get.

quiz.q: Which character has the fewest choices because she has so little money?
quiz.explain: Mrs Johnstone is poor, which is why she gives away a twin. This links to class and gender.

writing_intro: Use PEA paragraphs: Point, Evidence, Analysis. Use your booklet to find the evidence. Type your own quotation from the extract on page 5.

PEA.E: Copy a short quotation from the extract on page 5 of your booklet that supports your point.
PEA.X: Name the technique. Say what one word suggests. Explain why it proves your point.

rag_topics.label: Key characters: Mickey, Eddie, Mrs Johnstone, Linda
Key themes: class, hope, gender, nature vs nurture

learn.title: The play
learn.text: Blood Brothers is a musical play by Willy Russell, set in Liverpool. Mrs Johnstone, a poor mother, gives one of her newborn twins to Mrs Lyons, a rich woman she cleans for.

learn.title: The twins
learn.text: Mickey grows up poor with Mrs Johnstone. Eddie grows up rich with the Lyons family. They meet at seven and become 'blood brothers', without knowing they are twins.

learn.title: The others
learn.text: Linda is a friend to both twins and marries Mickey. Sammy is Mickey's older brother, who leads him into crime. The Narrator keeps reminding the audience how the story will end.

learn.title: Class
learn.text: Money shapes the twins' lives. Eddie goes to university and gets a good job. Mickey loses his job, goes to prison and becomes depressed.

learn.title: Nature vs nurture
learn.text: The twins are born the same (nature) but grow up in different homes (nurture). The play suggests that upbringing shapes who you become.

learn.title: Hope and gender
learn.text: Characters hope for a better life, but class and money crush those hopes. Women such as Mrs Johnstone and Linda have few choices and depend on men and money.

learn.title: Repetition and emotive language
learn.text: Repetition uses the same word more than once to make it stand out. Emotive language uses words chosen to make us feel something strongly, such as sadness or anger.

learn.title: Metaphor and simile
learn.text: A metaphor says something is something else: 'The classroom was a zoo.' A simile compares using 'like' or 'as': 'as cold as ice'.

learn.title: Direct address and ellipsis
learn.text: Direct address speaks straight to someone, often using 'you'. An ellipsis (…) shows words left out or a thought trailing off.

learn.title: Foreshadowing
learn.text: Foreshadowing is a hint early in a story about what will happen later. In Blood Brothers, the Narrator tells us how it ends at the very start.

learn.title: Dramatic irony
learn.text: Dramatic irony is when the audience knows something a character does not. We know Mickey and Eddie are twins, but they do not.

learn.title: The scene
learn.text: In the extract on page 5, Mrs Johnstone enters pushing a pram. She sings about money, debts and things that can be taken back, and about a baby she must not get attached to.

learn.title: Sympathy
learn.text: Sympathy means feeling sorry for a character. Russell makes us feel for Mrs Johnstone through her money worries, her love for the baby, repetition, direct address and the ellipsis at the end.

learn.title: PEA paragraphs
learn.text: Point: answer the question. Evidence: copy a short quote from the extract. Analysis: name the technique and say what one word suggests. Use the writing builder to practise the page 5 question.
